title: Polite bulk domain checks in Python with asyncio and a semaphore
summary:
Bulk domain checks (DNS, HTTP status, robots.txt, WHOIS) are mostly waiting on the network. Running them one by one wastes time, but firing 2,000 requests at once gets you rate-limited, blocked, or timing out. asyncio with a semaphore is the simple middle ground.

The pattern 

import asyncio
import aiohttp

LIMIT = 20          # max requests in flight
TIMEOUT = aiohttp.ClientTimeout(total=15)

async def check(session, sem, domain):
    url = f"https://{domain}/"
    async with sem:
        try:
            async with session.get(url, allow_redirects=True) as r:
                return domain, r.status, str(r.url)
        except Exception as e:
            return domain, None, type(e).__name__

async def main(domains):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(LIMIT)
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession(timeout=TIMEOUT) as session:
        tasks = [check(session, sem, d) for d in domains]
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

domains = [line.strip() for line in open("domains.txt") if line.strip()]
for domain, status, final in asyncio.run(main(domains)):
    print(domain, status, final)

All tasks are created up front, but the semaphore only lets 20 of them hold a connection at a time. The rest wait their turn without blocking the event loop.

Be polite per host, not just globally

A global limit of 20 can still send 20 requests to the same host if your list has many URLs from one site. Add a per-host semaphore:

from collections import defaultdict
from urllib.parse import urlparse

host_sems = defaultdict(lambda: asyncio.Semaphore(2))

async def check(session, sem, url):
    host = urlparse(url).netloc
    async with sem, host_sems[host]:
        ...

Two concurrent requests per host is a reasonable default for audits.

Add a small delay and retries 

async def fetch_with_retry(session, url, tries=3):
    for attempt in range(tries):
        try:
            async with session.get(url) as r:
                return r.status
        except (aiohttp.ClientError, asyncio.TimeoutError):
            await asyncio.sleep(1.5 * (attempt + 1))
    return None

Back-off between retries avoids hammering a host that is already struggling.

Practical numbers

  • 15 second total timeout per request is plenty; slow sites are rarely worth waiting longer for.
  • Keep LIMIT between 10 and 50 from a home connection.
  • Always set a clear User-Agent if you check many sites, so admins can identify the traffic.

Where this fits

I use this kind of script for the technical part of a prospect audit: which domains resolve, redirect, or return errors. Authority and spam metrics are a separate step; for those I use a bulk lookup such as DAPA Checker rather than scraping anything.

Python docs for asyncio.Semaphore: https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-sync.html#asyncio.Semaphore

title: Implied Probability, Fee Drag & Fractional Kelly Sizing in Binary Event Markets
summary:
Binary prediction contracts quote prices from 1¢ to 99¢ that look deceptively like pure probabilities. Yet between order-book spread, taker fees, and exit slippage, a raw 4-point discrepancy between two venues can easily carry negative expected value once execution friction is accounted for.

“Edge is never the gap between your opinion and the last traded price—it is what survives after round-trip execution drag and estimation error.”

— Luca Automated Studio Notes

01 · Converting Contract Price Into Fee-Adjusted Break-Even

When a YES contract trades at 0.42 ($0.42 on a $1.00 payout), the naive implied probability is 42.0%. However, if crossing the spread and accounting for settlement/exchange drag adds 0.015 (1.5 percentage points) to effective entry cost, your true break-even win rate rises to 43.5%. Any model estimate below that threshold loses capital over repeated trials even when directionally plausible.

To make this check instantaneous, we released our browser-based Implied Probability & Fractional Kelly Calculator inside Luca Labs.

02 · Why Full Kelly Fails Under Parameter Uncertainty

In textbook coin-flip examples, the true probability p is known with certainty. In real event markets—macro policy decisions, earnings catalysts, or geopolitical timelines—your calibrated probability is itself a distribution with estimation variance. Applying full Kelly sizing to noisy probability estimates exposes a portfolio to severe drawdown asymmetry.

  • Quarter-Kelly (0.25x): Captures roughly 44% of theoretical logarithmic growth while cutting variance dramatically.

  • Hard Execution Floor: Stand aside whenever estimated edge after fees falls inside normal order-book noise.

  • Cross-Venue Confirmation: Compare retail-dominated liquidity pools against institutional order books, as explored in our Cross-Venue Dispersion Study.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

Key Studio Takeaways

How do you calculate break-even probability on a binary prediction contract?

Add your realistic round-trip spread and fee drag directly to the quoted contract price (between 0 and 1). A 42-cent contract with 1.5 cents of friction requires a 43.5% true win rate just to break even.

Why do quantitative researchers use Fractional Kelly instead of Full Kelly?

Because real-world probability estimates contain model error. Quarter-Kelly (0.25x) protects against over-betting when true event odds are slightly lower than estimated.

title: How You Can Run Massive LLMs Even on Consumer Hardware (5 Bottlenecks, Simple Fixes & Step-by-Step Code)
summary:
You see an exciting new 35B or 300B+ open-source AI model drop on HuggingFace.

You open your laptop, your gaming PC with an 8 GB–16 GB GPU, or a free Google Colab T4, run AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...)—and within seconds your terminal explodes with:

RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory.

Or worse, your system RAM hits 100%, swap kicks in, and your entire computer freezes before generating a single word.

Most people assume you need $30,000 enterprise GPUs to run big Large Language Models. You don't.

Running a massive modern LLM on consumer hardware isn't blocked by one impossible wall—it's blocked by 5 small, surprisingly simple software mistakes that standard loaders make by default.

In this guide, we'll break down each of those 5 small bottlenecks one by one:

  1. The Simple Problem (in plain English + 1-line math)
  2. The Simple Fix (how to rethink it)
  3. Step-by-Step Python Code (clean, readable code showing exactly how it works)

At the end, you'll also see how to run all of this out-of-the-box in 3 commands—running a 35-Billion-parameter model inside 2.7 GB of GPU VRAM at 30 tokens/sec (or 43 tokens/sec on a 15 GB T4), and even a 306-Billion-parameter model on a single GPU.

Bottleneck 1: Python Crashes Before Reading Any Weights

The Simple Problem

When you initialize a PyTorch model the normal way (model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_config(config)), PyTorch immediately allocates random 32-bit numbers in your RAM for every single parameter before it even opens your downloaded weights file.

  • The Math: 35 Billion parameters × 4 bytes (float32) = 140 GB of useless random numbers!
  • Even a 32 GB PC crashes before loading byte #1 from disk.

The Simple Fix

Build the model on PyTorch's "meta" device first. A meta model is just an empty architectural blueprint—it knows every layer's shape and connections, while using literally 0 bytes of RAM and 0 bytes of GPU VRAM. Then you stream real 4-bit or 16-bit weights into it piece by piece.

Step-by-Step Code 

import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM

def create_zero_ram_skeleton(model_id: str):
    # Step 1: Download ONLY the tiny JSON config (~5 KB), not the 70 GB weights
    config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)

    # Step 2: Build the entire neural network inside PyTorch's "meta" device.
    # Memory used on CPU RAM = 0 bytes! Memory used on GPU VRAM = 0 bytes!
    with torch.device("meta"):
        model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_config(
            config,
            dtype=torch.float16,   # Keep default blueprint in 16-bit, NOT 32-bit!
            trust_remote_code=True,
        )

    return model

Why this works: Instead of needing 140 GB of upfront scratch RAM just to construct the Python object, create_zero_ram_skeleton() finishes in milliseconds using 0 MB.

Bottleneck 2: Your Vocabulary Table Wastes 1–2 GB of GPU VRAM

The Simple Problem

Modern 2026 LLMs support 150,000 to 250,000 tokens (words/subwords across dozens of languages and code).
If vocab_size = 248,320 and hidden_size = 4,096, that first lookup table (embed_tokens) takes:

  • The Math: 248,320 × 4,096 × 2 bytes (FP16) ≈ 2.03 GB of GPU VRAM!
  • The Irony: To generate the next word, the GPU only looks up 1 single row (8 KB) out of those 248,320 rows! Keeping 2 GB parked on a 6 GB or 8 GB GPU just to read 8 KB per token is pure waste.

The Simple Fix

Keep embed_tokens.bin on disk/RAM using operating-system memory mapping (mmap). Let the CPU grab just the 8 KB row for the current token ID and copy only those 8 KB to the GPU. GPU VRAM used = 0 MB.

Step-by-Step Code 

import mmap
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class ZeroVramMmapEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, bin_path: str, vocab_size: int, hidden_size: int, device: str = "cuda"):
        super().__init__()
        self.device = device
        # Step 1: Open the raw FP16 embedding file WITHOUT loading it into RAM
        self._file = open(bin_path, "rb")
        self._mmap = mmap.mmap(self._file.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ)

        # Step 2: Wrap the mmap buffer as a zero-copy 2D NumPy view [vocab_size, hidden_size]
        self.table = np.frombuffer(
            self._mmap, dtype=np.float16, count=vocab_size * hidden_size
        ).reshape(vocab_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, input_ids: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # Step 3: Pull token IDs to CPU (usually just 1 integer during generation!)
        ids_cpu = input_ids.detach().cpu().numpy()

        # Step 4: Slice ONLY the needed 8 KB row(s) and send that tiny slice to the GPU
        rows = np.ascontiguousarray(self.table[ids_cpu])
        return torch.from_numpy(rows).to(self.device, non_blocking=True)

Result: You instantly save 1 GB to 2 GB of GPU VRAM with virtually zero speed penalty (8 KB takes < 0.002 ms to copy).

Bottleneck 3: Loading All "Experts" When Each Word Uses Only 3%

The Simple Problem

Almost every frontier open model today (Qwen3.6, DeepSeek-V3/V4, GLM-5, Llama-4, Mixtral) uses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE).

Think of an MoE model like a hospital with 256 specialist doctors ("experts") on every floor, where each patient (token) only visits 8 doctors (3.1%):

  • A 35B model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) only activates 3B parameters per word!
  • Yet standard tools try to load all 256 experts onto your GPU—or offload entire floors to the CPU (llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe), leaving half your GPU sitting idle or crashing with OOM on 288-expert models.

The Simple Fix

Instead of keeping all 256 experts in a layer or zero experts in a layer, give every layer a small "VIP Parking Lot" (Slot Arena) in GPU VRAM—say 16 or 32 slots per layer.

In natural human language (or Python code), a small group of popular experts gets picked over and over again. Tracking popularity with a simple frequency counter (TinyLFU) lets just 25%–50% of slots answer 70% to 88% of expert lookups directly on the GPU!

Step-by-Step Code 

class LayerSlotCache:
    """Tracks which experts live inside a fixed-size GPU VRAM slot arena."""

    def __init__(self, num_slots: int, num_experts: int):
        # Step 1: Map expert_id -> gpu_slot (-1 means NOT currently on GPU)
        self.expert_to_slot = [-1] * num_experts
        self.slot_to_expert = [-1] * num_slots
        # Step 2: Count how often each expert is actually requested by the router
        self.freq = [0] * num_experts

    def split_hits_and_misses(self, selected_experts: list[int]):
        gpu_hits, cpu_misses = [], []

        for eid in selected_experts:
            self.freq[eid] += 1                      # Step 3: Record popularity
            slot = self.expert_to_slot[eid]
            if slot != -1:
                gpu_hits.append((eid, slot))         # Fast path: already in GPU VRAM!
            else:
                cpu_misses.append(eid)               # Cold path: not in VRAM right now

        return gpu_hits, cpu_misses

    def maybe_promote(self, cold_eid: int) -> int | None:
        # Step 4: Find the least-used expert currently parked on the GPU
        victim_slot = min(
            range(len(self.slot_to_expert)),
            key=lambda s: self.freq[self.slot_to_expert[s]] if self.slot_to_expert[s] != -1 else -1,
        )
        resident_eid = self.slot_to_expert[victim_slot]

        # Step 5: Only replace it if the new expert is strictly MORE popular!
        if resident_eid == -1 or self.freq[cold_eid] > self.freq[resident_eid]:
            if resident_eid != -1:
                self.expert_to_slot[resident_eid] = -1
            self.slot_to_expert[victim_slot] = cold_eid
            self.expert_to_slot[cold_eid] = victim_slot
            return victim_slot
        return None

Why this works: Random one-off experts don't kick out your hot coding/conversation experts. Your GPU VRAM usage stays 100% flat and predictable—whether you give it 2.7 GB (8 slots/layer) or 12 GB (159 slots/layer).

Bottleneck 4: The PCIe Cable Traffic Jam (8 KB vs 13.5 MB!)

The Simple Problem

Here is the biggest trap people fall into when building "weight streaming" engines:

"Whenever a needed expert isn't in GPU VRAM, I'll just copy its weights from CPU RAM to GPU VRAM, run it, and move on!"

Let's check the math over a normal PCIe cable (~12–16 GB/s real-world speed):

  • 1 single large expert's weights (4-bit): ~2 MB to 13.5 MB
  • Across 40 layers (2–5 misses per layer): 200 MB to 3,000 MB copied for every single word!
  • Your GPU spends 90% of its life stalled waiting on the PCIe cable, crawling at 2–4 tokens/sec.

The Simple Fix

Never move missed expert weights to the GPU during token generation. Move the tiny token vector to the CPU instead!

Look at the size difference:

  • Moving the expert weights to the GPU = 13,500 KB per miss.
  • Moving the token hidden state to the CPU = 8 KB (4096 × 2 bytes)!

While the GPU computes all the cached Hit experts, your multi-core CPU simultaneously multiplies that 8 KB vector against the Missed experts directly over mmap in RAM, and sends a single 8 KB result vector back to add on the GPU!

           GPU (VRAM Slot Arena)                        CPU (Multi-Core SIMD over mmap)
   +-----------------------------------+        +-------------------------------------+
   | 1. Attention + Router             |        |                                     |
   | 2. Send 8 KB vector + Miss IDs ---+------->| 3. Run ONLY Missed Experts in RAM   |
   | 4. Run Cached Hit Experts on GPU  |  8 KB  |    (Zero weight copies over PCIe!)  |
   | 5. Final Output = GPU + CPU <-----+--------+ 4. Return 8 KB vector to GPU        |
   +-----------------------------------+  8 KB  +-------------------------------------+

Step-by-Step Code 

import torch

def hybrid_moe_forward(
    x_gpu: torch.Tensor,              # Shape: [1, hidden_size] (~8 KB in FP16)
    routed_ids: list[int],            # e.g. 8 chosen experts out of 256
    routed_weights: torch.Tensor,     # Router probabilities
    cache: LayerSlotCache,
    gpu_slot_arena,                   # Fast 4-bit GPU kernel on resident slots
    cpu_mmap_pool,                    # Parallel C++/SIMD threads over mmap file
) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Step 1: Split the 8 chosen experts into GPU Hits vs CPU Misses
    hits, misses = cache.split_hits_and_misses(routed_ids)

    # Step 2: Copy ONLY the tiny 8 KB activation vector to CPU (NOT megabytes of weights!)
    if misses:
        x_cpu = x_gpu.to("cpu", non_blocking=True)

    # Step 3: Launch GPU kernel for all cached Hits immediately (non-blocking)
    y_gpu = gpu_slot_arena.run_4bit_swiglu(x_gpu, hits, routed_weights)

    # Step 4: At the SAME TIME, CPU computes any Misses in-place over mmap
    if misses:
        y_cpu = cpu_mmap_pool.run_4bit_misses(x_cpu, misses, routed_weights)
        # Send just 8 KB back to GPU and sum the two partial answers!
        y_gpu = y_gpu + y_cpu.to(x_gpu.device, non_blocking=True)

        # Optional Step 5: Promote at most 1 newly hot expert in background DMA stream
        cache.maybe_promote(misses[0])

    return y_gpu

Result: On a 35B MoE model on an NVIDIA T4, eliminating PCIe weight stalls jumped speed from 5.3 tokens/sec -> 43.3 tokens/sec (8x faster) with zero loss in output quality!

Bottleneck 5: Running a 21 GB Model on a 12 GB RAM Machine (Stopping OS Double-Caching)

The Simple Problem

What if your quantized model is 21 GB (or 186 GB), and your system RAM is only 12 GB (like free Colab or a budget PC)?

When you read 10 GB of popular experts from your SSD via mmap and upload them into GPU VRAM, your operating system tries to be "helpful" and keeps a duplicate copy of those exact same 10 GB in system RAM (the OS file page cache).

  • Now 10 GB of GPU VRAM + 10 GB of System RAM hold the exact same data!
  • Your remaining RAM runs out, and your SSD starts thrashing violently.

(Bonus Linux gotcha: Python/C's standard posix_madvise(..., POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED) is actually a **silent no-op* in Linux glibc—it returns 0 without freeing a single byte!)*

The Simple Fix

Pack each expert aligned to 16 KB OS memory pages. The exact millisecond an expert finishes copying into GPU VRAM, call the raw Linux madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) syscall on that expert's slice so the OS drops the duplicate RAM pages immediately.

Now your GPU VRAM holds hot experts and your System RAM holds only non-overlapping cold experts!

Step-by-Step Code 

import ctypes
import sys

MADV_DONTNEED = 4  # Linux kernel constant: "drop these clean file pages from RAM now"
_libc = ctypes.CDLL("libc.so.6") if sys.platform.startswith("linux") else None

def drop_duplicate_ram_pages(mmap_base_addr: int, expert_offset: int, expert_bytes: int) -> None:
    """Free Host RAM pages immediately after an expert is uploaded into GPU VRAM."""
    if _libc is None:
        return

    # Step 1: Must be aligned to OS page size (4 KB on x86 Linux, 16 KB on ARM/macOS)
    page_addr = mmap_base_addr + expert_offset

    # Step 2: Call raw Linux madvise() directly (NOT glibc's no-op posix_madvise!)
    # Because cas_experts_q4.bin is read-only on disk, the kernel safely frees the RAM
    # instantly and seamlessly re-reads from NVMe only if needed later.
    _libc.madvise(
        ctypes.c_void_p(page_addr),
        ctypes.c_size_t(expert_bytes),
        ctypes.c_int(MADV_DONTNEED),
    )

Result: With disjoint RAM + VRAM residency, a 21 GB 35B model runs smoothly inside a 12 GB RAM limit at 29.1 tokens/sec, and a 186 GB 306B model runs inside a 112 GB RAM limit (2.1x faster than llama.cpp)!

Try It Yourself in 3 Commands (Mac, Windows WSL2, Linux, or Colab)

We combined all 5 of these techniques—plus custom 4-bit CUDA __dp4a kernels, static CUDA Graphs, C++17 AVX2/NEON CPU pools, and native Apple Silicon Metal (MLX) kernels—into an open-source MIT engine: deimos-stream.

# 1. Install (Apple Silicon Mac uses native Metal MLX; Linux/WSL2 uses NVIDIA CUDA)

pip install -U "deimos-stream[cuda]"  # Linux / Windows WSL2 / Colab NVIDIA GPU

# 2. Stream-convert a HuggingFace MoE model into 16KB page-aligned 4-bit format

  --model-dir Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B \
  --output-dir ./qwen36_35b_q4

# 3. Chat! `--slots auto` automatically sizes the GPU slot cache to fit your free VRAM

  --store-dir ./qwen36_35b_q4 \
  --backbone q4 \
  --slots auto \

event_model_payload.headline: How You Can Run Massive LLMs Even on Consumer Hardware (5 Bottlenecks, Simple Fixes & Step-by-Step Code)
event_model_payload.summary:
You see an exciting new 35B or 300B+ open-source AI model drop on HuggingFace.

You open your laptop, your gaming PC with an 8 GB–16 GB GPU, or a free Google Colab T4, run AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...)—and within seconds your terminal explodes with:

RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory.

Or worse, your system RAM hits 100%, swap kicks in, and your entire computer freezes before generating a single word.

Most people assume you need $30,000 enterprise GPUs to run big Large Language Models. You don't.

Running a massive modern LLM on consumer hardware isn't blocked by one impossible wall—it's blocked by 5 small, surprisingly simple software mistakes that standard loaders make by default.

In this guide, we'll break down each of those 5 small bottlenecks one by one:

  1. The Simple Problem (in plain English + 1-line math)
  2. The Simple Fix (how to rethink it)
  3. Step-by-Step Python Code (clean, readable code showing exactly how it works)

At the end, you'll also see how to run all of this out-of-the-box in 3 commands—running a 35-Billion-parameter model inside 2.7 GB of GPU VRAM at 30 tokens/sec (or 43 tokens/sec on a 15 GB T4), and even a 306-Billion-parameter model on a single GPU.

Bottleneck 1: Python Crashes Before Reading Any Weights

The Simple Problem

When you initialize a PyTorch model the normal way (model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_config(config)), PyTorch immediately allocates random 32-bit numbers in your RAM for every single parameter before it even opens your downloaded weights file.

  • The Math: 35 Billion parameters × 4 bytes (float32) = 140 GB of useless random numbers!
  • Even a 32 GB PC crashes before loading byte #1 from disk.

The Simple Fix

Build the model on PyTorch's "meta" device first. A meta model is just an empty architectural blueprint—it knows every layer's shape and connections, while using literally 0 bytes of RAM and 0 bytes of GPU VRAM. Then you stream real 4-bit or 16-bit weights into it piece by piece.

Step-by-Step Code 

import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM

def create_zero_ram_skeleton(model_id: str):
    # Step 1: Download ONLY the tiny JSON config (~5 KB), not the 70 GB weights
    config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)

    # Step 2: Build the entire neural network inside PyTorch's "meta" device.
    # Memory used on CPU RAM = 0 bytes! Memory used on GPU VRAM = 0 bytes!
    with torch.device("meta"):
        model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_config(
            config,
            dtype=torch.float16,   # Keep default blueprint in 16-bit, NOT 32-bit!
            trust_remote_code=True,
        )

    return model

Why this works: Instead of needing 140 GB of upfront scratch RAM just to construct the Python object, create_zero_ram_skeleton() finishes in milliseconds using 0 MB.

Bottleneck 2: Your Vocabulary Table Wastes 1–2 GB of GPU VRAM

The Simple Problem

Modern 2026 LLMs support 150,000 to 250,000 tokens (words/subwords across dozens of languages and code).
If vocab_size = 248,320 and hidden_size = 4,096, that first lookup table (embed_tokens) takes:

  • The Math: 248,320 × 4,096 × 2 bytes (FP16) ≈ 2.03 GB of GPU VRAM!
  • The Irony: To generate the next word, the GPU only looks up 1 single row (8 KB) out of those 248,320 rows! Keeping 2 GB parked on a 6 GB or 8 GB GPU just to read 8 KB per token is pure waste.

The Simple Fix

Keep embed_tokens.bin on disk/RAM using operating-system memory mapping (mmap). Let the CPU grab just the 8 KB row for the current token ID and copy only those 8 KB to the GPU. GPU VRAM used = 0 MB.

Step-by-Step Code 

import mmap
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class ZeroVramMmapEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, bin_path: str, vocab_size: int, hidden_size: int, device: str = "cuda"):
        super().__init__()
        self.device = device
        # Step 1: Open the raw FP16 embedding file WITHOUT loading it into RAM
        self._file = open(bin_path, "rb")
        self._mmap = mmap.mmap(self._file.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ)

        # Step 2: Wrap the mmap buffer as a zero-copy 2D NumPy view [vocab_size, hidden_size]
        self.table = np.frombuffer(
            self._mmap, dtype=np.float16, count=vocab_size * hidden_size
        ).reshape(vocab_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, input_ids: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # Step 3: Pull token IDs to CPU (usually just 1 integer during generation!)
        ids_cpu = input_ids.detach().cpu().numpy()

        # Step 4: Slice ONLY the needed 8 KB row(s) and send that tiny slice to the GPU
        rows = np.ascontiguousarray(self.table[ids_cpu])
        return torch.from_numpy(rows).to(self.device, non_blocking=True)

Result: You instantly save 1 GB to 2 GB of GPU VRAM with virtually zero speed penalty (8 KB takes < 0.002 ms to copy).

Bottleneck 3: Loading All "Experts" When Each Word Uses Only 3%

The Simple Problem

Almost every frontier open model today (Qwen3.6, DeepSeek-V3/V4, GLM-5, Llama-4, Mixtral) uses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE).

Think of an MoE model like a hospital with 256 specialist doctors ("experts") on every floor, where each patient (token) only visits 8 doctors (3.1%):

  • A 35B model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) only activates 3B parameters per word!
  • Yet standard tools try to load all 256 experts onto your GPU—or offload entire floors to the CPU (llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe), leaving half your GPU sitting idle or crashing with OOM on 288-expert models.

The Simple Fix

Instead of keeping all 256 experts in a layer or zero experts in a layer, give every layer a small "VIP Parking Lot" (Slot Arena) in GPU VRAM—say 16 or 32 slots per layer.

In natural human language (or Python code), a small group of popular experts gets picked over and over again. Tracking popularity with a simple frequency counter (TinyLFU) lets just 25%–50% of slots answer 70% to 88% of expert lookups directly on the GPU!

Step-by-Step Code 

class LayerSlotCache:
    """Tracks which experts live inside a fixed-size GPU VRAM slot arena."""

    def __init__(self, num_slots: int, num_experts: int):
        # Step 1: Map expert_id -> gpu_slot (-1 means NOT currently on GPU)
        self.expert_to_slot = [-1] * num_experts
        self.slot_to_expert = [-1] * num_slots
        # Step 2: Count how often each expert is actually requested by the router
        self.freq = [0] * num_experts

    def split_hits_and_misses(self, selected_experts: list[int]):
        gpu_hits, cpu_misses = [], []

        for eid in selected_experts:
            self.freq[eid] += 1                      # Step 3: Record popularity
            slot = self.expert_to_slot[eid]
            if slot != -1:
                gpu_hits.append((eid, slot))         # Fast path: already in GPU VRAM!
            else:
                cpu_misses.append(eid)               # Cold path: not in VRAM right now

        return gpu_hits, cpu_misses

    def maybe_promote(self, cold_eid: int) -> int | None:
        # Step 4: Find the least-used expert currently parked on the GPU
        victim_slot = min(
            range(len(self.slot_to_expert)),
            key=lambda s: self.freq[self.slot_to_expert[s]] if self.slot_to_expert[s] != -1 else -1,
        )
        resident_eid = self.slot_to_expert[victim_slot]

        # Step 5: Only replace it if the new expert is strictly MORE popular!
        if resident_eid == -1 or self.freq[cold_eid] > self.freq[resident_eid]:
            if resident_eid != -1:
                self.expert_to_slot[resident_eid] = -1
            self.slot_to_expert[victim_slot] = cold_eid
            self.expert_to_slot[cold_eid] = victim_slot
            return victim_slot
        return None

Why this works: Random one-off experts don't kick out your hot coding/conversation experts. Your GPU VRAM usage stays 100% flat and predictable—whether you give it 2.7 GB (8 slots/layer) or 12 GB (159 slots/layer).

Bottleneck 4: The PCIe Cable Traffic Jam (8 KB vs 13.5 MB!)

The Simple Problem

Here is the biggest trap people fall into when building "weight streaming" engines:

"Whenever a needed expert isn't in GPU VRAM, I'll just copy its weights from CPU RAM to GPU VRAM, run it, and move on!"

Let's check the math over a normal PCIe cable (~12–16 GB/s real-world speed):

  • 1 single large expert's weights (4-bit): ~2 MB to 13.5 MB
  • Across 40 layers (2–5 misses per layer): 200 MB to 3,000 MB copied for every single word!
  • Your GPU spends 90% of its life stalled waiting on the PCIe cable, crawling at 2–4 tokens/sec.

The Simple Fix

Never move missed expert weights to the GPU during token generation. Move the tiny token vector to the CPU instead!

Look at the size difference:

  • Moving the expert weights to the GPU = 13,500 KB per miss.
  • Moving the token hidden state to the CPU = 8 KB (4096 × 2 bytes)!

While the GPU computes all the cached Hit experts, your multi-core CPU simultaneously multiplies that 8 KB vector against the Missed experts directly over mmap in RAM, and sends a single 8 KB result vector back to add on the GPU!

           GPU (VRAM Slot Arena)                        CPU (Multi-Core SIMD over mmap)
   +-----------------------------------+        +-------------------------------------+
   | 1. Attention + Router             |        |                                     |
   | 2. Send 8 KB vector + Miss IDs ---+------->| 3. Run ONLY Missed Experts in RAM   |
   | 4. Run Cached Hit Experts on GPU  |  8 KB  |    (Zero weight copies over PCIe!)  |
   | 5. Final Output = GPU + CPU <-----+--------+ 4. Return 8 KB vector to GPU        |
   +-----------------------------------+  8 KB  +-------------------------------------+

Step-by-Step Code 

import torch

def hybrid_moe_forward(
    x_gpu: torch.Tensor,              # Shape: [1, hidden_size] (~8 KB in FP16)
    routed_ids: list[int],            # e.g. 8 chosen experts out of 256
    routed_weights: torch.Tensor,     # Router probabilities
    cache: LayerSlotCache,
    gpu_slot_arena,                   # Fast 4-bit GPU kernel on resident slots
    cpu_mmap_pool,                    # Parallel C++/SIMD threads over mmap file
) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Step 1: Split the 8 chosen experts into GPU Hits vs CPU Misses
    hits, misses = cache.split_hits_and_misses(routed_ids)

    # Step 2: Copy ONLY the tiny 8 KB activation vector to CPU (NOT megabytes of weights!)
    if misses:
        x_cpu = x_gpu.to("cpu", non_blocking=True)

    # Step 3: Launch GPU kernel for all cached Hits immediately (non-blocking)
    y_gpu = gpu_slot_arena.run_4bit_swiglu(x_gpu, hits, routed_weights)

    # Step 4: At the SAME TIME, CPU computes any Misses in-place over mmap
    if misses:
        y_cpu = cpu_mmap_pool.run_4bit_misses(x_cpu, misses, routed_weights)
        # Send just 8 KB back to GPU and sum the two partial answers!
        y_gpu = y_gpu + y_cpu.to(x_gpu.device, non_blocking=True)

        # Optional Step 5: Promote at most 1 newly hot expert in background DMA stream
        cache.maybe_promote(misses[0])

    return y_gpu

Result: On a 35B MoE model on an NVIDIA T4, eliminating PCIe weight stalls jumped speed from 5.3 tokens/sec -> 43.3 tokens/sec (8x faster) with zero loss in output quality!

Bottleneck 5: Running a 21 GB Model on a 12 GB RAM Machine (Stopping OS Double-Caching)

The Simple Problem

What if your quantized model is 21 GB (or 186 GB), and your system RAM is only 12 GB (like free Colab or a budget PC)?

When you read 10 GB of popular experts from your SSD via mmap and upload them into GPU VRAM, your operating system tries to be "helpful" and keeps a duplicate copy of those exact same 10 GB in system RAM (the OS file page cache).

  • Now 10 GB of GPU VRAM + 10 GB of System RAM hold the exact same data!
  • Your remaining RAM runs out, and your SSD starts thrashing violently.

(Bonus Linux gotcha: Python/C's standard posix_madvise(..., POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED) is actually a **silent no-op* in Linux glibc—it returns 0 without freeing a single byte!)*

The Simple Fix

Pack each expert aligned to 16 KB OS memory pages. The exact millisecond an expert finishes copying into GPU VRAM, call the raw Linux madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) syscall on that expert's slice so the OS drops the duplicate RAM pages immediately.

Now your GPU VRAM holds hot experts and your System RAM holds only non-overlapping cold experts!

Step-by-Step Code 

import ctypes
import sys

MADV_DONTNEED = 4  # Linux kernel constant: "drop these clean file pages from RAM now"
_libc = ctypes.CDLL("libc.so.6") if sys.platform.startswith("linux") else None

def drop_duplicate_ram_pages(mmap_base_addr: int, expert_offset: int, expert_bytes: int) -> None:
    """Free Host RAM pages immediately after an expert is uploaded into GPU VRAM."""
    if _libc is None:
        return

    # Step 1: Must be aligned to OS page size (4 KB on x86 Linux, 16 KB on ARM/macOS)
    page_addr = mmap_base_addr + expert_offset

    # Step 2: Call raw Linux madvise() directly (NOT glibc's no-op posix_madvise!)
    # Because cas_experts_q4.bin is read-only on disk, the kernel safely frees the RAM
    # instantly and seamlessly re-reads from NVMe only if needed later.
    _libc.madvise(
        ctypes.c_void_p(page_addr),
        ctypes.c_size_t(expert_bytes),
        ctypes.c_int(MADV_DONTNEED),
    )

Result: With disjoint RAM + VRAM residency, a 21 GB 35B model runs smoothly inside a 12 GB RAM limit at 29.1 tokens/sec, and a 186 GB 306B model runs inside a 112 GB RAM limit (2.1x faster than llama.cpp)!

title: Adding OpenTelemetry tracing to a Django app (and finding an N+1 in SigNoz)
summary:
Adding OpenTelemetry tracing to a Django app (and finding an N+1 in SigNoz)

When a Django page is slow, logs tell you that it was slow. A trace tells you where: which view, which SQL query, which outbound call. OpenTelemetry (OTel) gives you traces in a vendor-neutral format, and the Python agent can instrument Django and PostgreSQL without you editing your views.

In this guide you will:

  1. Trace a small Django + PostgreSQL app with no code changes.
  2. Add one custom span with useful attributes.
  3. Spot an N+1 query in a trace, fix it, and compare.
  4. Run it under Gunicorn, correlate logs with traces, and cut noise with sampling.
  5. Send everything to SigNoz, an OpenTelemetry-native backend.

Everything below was run against a throwaway project: Python 3.13, Django 6.1, opentelemetry-sdk 1.45.2 with instrumentation packages 0.66b2, Gunicorn 27, psycopg2-binary 2.9.13 and a local PostgreSQL. Package versions move quickly, so check the release notes if something differs.

The demo app

A bookings app with two models and four endpoints:

# bookings/models.py
from django.db import models


class Customer(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)


class Booking(models.Model):
    customer = models.ForeignKey(Customer, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    starts_at = models.DateTimeField()
    confirmed = models.BooleanField(default=False)

# bookings/views.py
import logging
import time

from django.http import JsonResponse
from opentelemetry import trace

from .models import Booking

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)


def health(request):
    return JsonResponse({"ok": True})


def slow_list(request):
    """N+1 on purpose: one query for bookings, then one per customer."""
    rows = [
        {"id": b.id, "customer": b.customer.name}
        for b in Booking.objects.all()[:20]
    ]
    return JsonResponse({"count": len(rows), "rows": rows})


def fast_list(request):
    rows = [
        {"id": b.id, "customer": b.customer.name}
        for b in Booking.objects.select_related("customer")[:20]
    ]
    return JsonResponse({"count": len(rows), "rows": rows})


def confirm(request, booking_id):
    booking = Booking.objects.get(pk=booking_id)
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("confirm-booking") as span:
        span.set_attribute("booking.id", booking.id)
        span.set_attribute("booking.already_confirmed", booking.confirmed)
        time.sleep(0.05)  # stand-in for a payment or WhatsApp call
        logger.info("confirming booking %s", booking.id)
        booking.confirmed = True
        booking.save(update_fields=["confirmed"])
    return JsonResponse({"id": booking.id, "confirmed": True})

# shop/urls.py
from django.urls import path

from bookings import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("health/", views.health),
    path("bookings/slow/", views.slow_list),
    path("bookings/fast/", views.fast_list),
    path("bookings//confirm/", views.confirm),
]

Note that opentelemetry-api is the only OTel import in the views, and it is a no-op until an SDK is configured. Your app can ship the same code in every environment.

Step 1: zero-code tracing

Install the distro, the OTLP exporter, and the instrumentation packages that match what is installed in your virtualenv:

pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
opentelemetry-bootstrap --action=install

opentelemetry-bootstrap inspects your environment and installs the matching instrumentations. Run it after installing your app's dependencies. In this project it picked up Django, psycopg2, WSGI, and logging among others.

Before sending anything anywhere, print spans to the terminal:

export DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=shop.settings
export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=shop
export OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=console
export OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none
export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none

opentelemetry-instrument python manage.py runserver --noreload

--noreload matters. Django's autoreloader starts a child process, and the instrumentation does not carry over to it (SigNoz's Django guide has the same warning).

Hit /bookings/1/confirm/ and the console shows spans like these (trimmed):

SELECT   CLIENT    SELECT "bookings_booking"."id", ... WHERE "bookings_booking"."id" = %s LIMIT 21
UPDATE   CLIENT    UPDATE "bookings_booking" SET "confirmed" = %s WHERE ...
confirm-booking    INTERNAL   booking.id=1
GET bookings//confirm/   SERVER   http.route=..., http.status_code=200

That is a SERVER span for the request (named from the URL route, not the raw path, so cardinality stays low), CLIENT spans for each SQL statement with db.system=postgresql, and your own span nested inside. All of them share one trace ID.

Step 2: a custom span that earns its place

Auto-instrumentation sees HTTP and SQL. It cannot see your business meaning. That is what the confirm-booking span in the view is for: it wraps the part that talks to something slow, and it carries attributes you will actually filter by later (booking.id, booking.already_confirmed).

Two rules that keep this useful:

  • Attribute names are an API. Pick a prefix (booking.) and stay consistent.
  • No personal data in attributes. Use IDs, not names, emails or phone numbers. Traces are usually retained and shared more widely than your database.

Step 3: find the N+1

Call the two list endpoints and compare the traces:

curl localhost:8000/bookings/slow/
curl localhost:8000/bookings/fast/

In the demo data (10 bookings), /bookings/slow/ produced one query for the bookings and then ten identical SELECT ... FROM "bookings_customer" WHERE "id" = %s LIMIT 21 spans, one per row. /bookings/fast/ produced a single joined query. In a trace waterfall the slow version looks like a comb: ten short, identical bars in a row.

The fix is the usual one:

Booking.objects.select_related("customer")[:20]

The point is not that N+1s are new. It is that a trace shows you the count and the repeated statement text without you adding print or turning on query logging.

Step 4: Gunicorn in production

Django's runserver is for development. Under Gunicorn, the agent wraps the server command the same way:

opentelemetry-instrument gunicorn shop.wsgi --workers 2 --bind 0.0.0.0:8000

You may have read that OTel's background exporter thread is not fork-safe and that you need a post_fork hook. I tested the plain command above against a local OTLP receiver, both with and without --preload, and spans from all requests (including the SQL spans) arrived. If you want explicit control, for example a per-worker service.instance.id, this hook works too:

# gunicorn.conf.py
import os


def post_fork(server, worker):
    """Runs in every worker right after fork, before the app is loaded."""
    from opentelemetry import trace
    from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter
    from opentelemetry.instrumentation.django import DjangoInstrumentor
    from opentelemetry.instrumentation.psycopg2 import Psycopg2Instrumentor
    from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource
    from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
    from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor

    resource = Resource.create(
        {
            "service.name": os.environ.get("OTEL_SERVICE_NAME", "shop"),
            "service.instance.id": f"gunicorn-{worker.pid}",
        }
    )
    provider = TracerProvider(resource=resource)
    provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter()))
    trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)

    DjangoInstrumentor().instrument()
    Psycopg2Instrumentor().instrument()

Run this with plain gunicorn shop.wsgi (Gunicorn picks up gunicorn.conf.py from the current directory). Do not combine it with opentelemetry-instrument: the agent sets a tracer provider in the master process first, and OTel refuses to replace a provider once one is set, so your hook's exporter is silently ignored. title: How to Find Your Singing Range With Python: Pitch Tracking From Scratch in Under 50 Lines
summary:
By Tania Alwan

Singers usually learn how to find their singing range with a piano: sing down until your voice gives out, sing up until it cracks, write down the two notes. It works, but it depends on your ear and on someone pressing keys.

A pitch tracker does the same job from a recording. In this post I build a small one in plain NumPy (no audio libraries), explain each step, and turn the output into a lowest note, a highest note and a more useful "comfortable range".

What "singing range" means in numbers

Every sung note has a fundamental frequency (f0), measured in hertz. A4 is 440 Hz by convention, and each semitone multiplies the frequency by 2^(1/12). That gives a direct formula from frequency to MIDI note number:

midi = 69 + 12 * log2(f / 440)

MIDI 69 is A4, 60 is middle C (C4). So finding your singing range is really two steps: estimate f0 over time, then convert the lowest and highest values to note names.

Step 1: record a siren

Record yourself gliding slowly from your lowest comfortable note to your highest and back, on a vowel like "oo" or a lip trill. Use a quiet room, a phone or USB mic at a steady distance, and export a mono WAV. Don't push to the point of strain: a tracker will happily measure a painful squeak, and that is not a note you want to plan songs around.

Step 2: estimate pitch with autocorrelation

A sung note is periodic: the waveform roughly repeats every 1/f0 seconds. Autocorrelation compares a short frame with shifted copies of itself; the shift (lag) with the strongest match is the period.

import numpy as np

A4 = 440.0
NAMES = ["C", "C#", "D", "D#", "E", "F", "F#", "G", "G#", "A", "A#", "B"]

def hz_to_note(f):
    midi = int(round(69 + 12 * np.log2(f / A4)))
    return f"{NAMES[midi % 12]}{midi // 12 - 1}"

def frame_pitch(frame, sr, fmin=70.0, fmax=1100.0, threshold=0.5):
    """Autocorrelation pitch estimate for one frame, or None if unvoiced."""
    frame = frame - frame.mean()
    if np.sqrt(np.mean(frame ** 2)) < 0.01:  # too quiet: treat as silence
        return None
    ac = np.correlate(frame, frame, mode="full")[len(frame) - 1:]
    ac = ac / ac[0]
    lo, hi = int(sr / fmax), int(sr / fmin)
    lag = lo + int(np.argmax(ac[lo:hi]))
    if ac[lag] < threshold:  # weak periodicity: probably noise or breath
        return None
    return sr / lag

def pitch_track(signal, sr, frame_ms=40, hop_ms=10):
    n, h = int(sr * frame_ms / 1000), int(sr * hop_ms / 1000)
    out = []
    for start in range(0, len(signal) - n, h):
        f = frame_pitch(signal[start:start + n], sr)
        if f is not None:
            out.append(f)
    return np.array(out)

def singing_range(f0, low_pct=5, high_pct=95):
    """Comfortable range: ignore the extreme 5% at each end."""
    lo, hi = np.percentile(f0, [low_pct, high_pct])
    return hz_to_note(lo), hz_to_note(hi)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sr = 16000
    # Fake "siren": a voice-like tone gliding from about A2 (110 Hz) to A4 (440 Hz)
    t = np.linspace(0, 3, 3 * sr, endpoint=False)
    freq = 110 * 2 ** (2 * t / 3)
    phase = 2 * np.pi * np.cumsum(freq) / sr
    voice = 0.6 * np.sin(phase) + 0.3 * np.sin(2 * phase) + 0.1 * np.sin(3 * phase)
    f0 = pitch_track(voice, sr)
    print("frames with pitch:", len(f0))
    print("lowest / highest detected:", hz_to_note(f0.min()), hz_to_note(f0.max()))
    print("comfortable range (5th-95th percentile):", singing_range(f0))

Run it and the synthetic glide from A2 to A4 comes back as:

frames with pitch: 296
lowest / highest detected: A2 A4
comfortable range (5th-95th percentile): ('B2', 'G#4')

To use your own recording, load the WAV with the standard wave module or soundfile, convert it to a float array between -1 and 1, and pass it to pitch_track.

Step 3: why the code ignores some frames

Three guards keep the result honest:

  • Silence gate. Frames with very low RMS energy are skipped, so breaths and room noise don't count as notes.
  • Search window. fmin=70 and fmax=1100 Hz limit the lags we check. That roughly covers adult voices from a low bass to a high soprano. Widen it if your voice goes beyond.
  • Periodicity threshold. If the best normalized autocorrelation peak is below 0.5, the frame is probably noisy or breathy, so it's dropped.

Step 4: lowest note vs comfortable range

The absolute minimum and maximum are fragile: one octave error or one strained note moves them a lot. Percentiles are more stable. Taking the 5th and 95th percentile of all voiced frames gives a range you actually spent time in, which is closer to what a vocal coach means by a comfortable or usable range.

Known limitations

  • Octave errors. Autocorrelation sometimes locks onto twice the period and reports a note an octave low. Production trackers such as YIN and pYIN add extra steps to reduce this.
  • One voice only. This works on a solo, dry vocal. On a full mix you'd need to separate the vocal first.
  • Range isn't voice type. Two singers with the same range can be very different voice types; timbre and where the voice feels easy matter too.

Using the result

Once you know your comfortable range, you can choose keys that sit inside it. If you sing covers, compare it with the song's melody range: when a melody goes beyond your comfortable top note, transpose the song down rather than straining. A key detector such as the Voicestars BPM and key finder tells you the original key, so you know how many semitones to move.

Range also matters for AI voice work: if you sing a guide vocal for a voice model, you get cleaner results when you stay in your own easy register.

title: Extracting Prediction Confidence from Scikit-Learn Classifiers
summary:
QuackBuilds has released a new snippet: Scikit-Learn Classifier Prediction Confidence.

This tool addresses a common need when working with classification models: understanding how confident your model is about each individual prediction. While a classifier provides a predicted class, knowing the underlying probability can offer deeper insights into its performance and reliability.

The snippet demonstrates the process of extracting these prediction probabilities directly from a scikit-learn classifier. It shows how to access the confidence scores for each class, which can then be used to evaluate the model's certainty for its chosen output. Additionally, it includes methods to identify and flag predictions where the model's confidence is notably low. This feature is useful for pinpointing ambiguous cases or areas where the model might require further training or data.

This is intended for developers and data scientists who use scikit-learn for classification tasks and need to go beyond simple class labels to understand model behavior.

title: Make Job Cancellation a Durable State Transition
summary:
A worker has already claimed a report. An operator clicks Cancel. The worker finishes calculating a result a moment later.

What decides whether that result can become the saved result?

Checking a cancellation flag before calculation leaves a gap. The worker can pass that check, pause, and resume after cancellation has been accepted. Stopping the caller from waiting leaves the same gap in a different place.

This example makes cancellation a durable state transition. Once the cancellation transaction commits, the normal completion path can no longer publish a result for that run. The process may still be alive. An external request it already sent may still finish.

Give the command an exact run

The previous tutorial separated the stable job, an intentionally requested run, and the worker's claim generation. Cancellation needs that distinction too.

Use (job_id, run_id) as its target. If an old cancel request is retried after a new run starts, it must still address the old run. Resolving “the current run of this job” again during the retry would change the target.

The local fixture uses these transitions:

queued  -> running -> succeeded
   |          |
   +----------+----> cancelled

succeeded and cancelled are terminal for this execution. A deliberate rerun is a separate row. The fixture's cancelled state means the run's normal completion path is closed. It is not evidence that the worker exited or a remote operation was reversed.

Put cancellation and completion behind the same database boundary

Cancellation changes only a queued or running row with the exact job and run IDs. It also clears the current ownership fields.

Completion must still match:

  • The exact job and run.
  • The running state.
  • The worker and generation from the originally issued claim.
  • An unexpired lease.

Those predicates are evaluated inside the completion write. A previous application-level read is not permission to skip them.

The two commands can race. The API needs to describe both possible results:

First transition to commit Later command observes Saved result
Cancellation Completion is refused None
Completion Cancellation returns succeeded, with changed=False Original completed result

The caller does not get a successful cancellation merely because it pressed Cancel first. In this fixture, the database's committed order determines which transition wins.

If cancellation commits but its response disappears, repeating the same job/run cancellation returns cancelled with changed=False. It does not start another execution, delete a completed result, or retarget a newer run.

Keep protocol cancellation separate

The MCP cancellation specification, revision 2026-07-28 describes transport-specific cancellation signals and races with completed requests. It also permits a server to ignore a cancellation notification when the request has completed or cannot be cancelled.

A request ID identifies a protocol exchange. The run ID below identifies a durable execution. An application that connects them needs an explicit mapping and authorization check; a disconnected client is not proof that a business job has been cancelled or rolled back.

This tutorial implements a local job-state contract, not an MCP transport or notification handler.

Run the complete fixture

Save the file as cancel_fence.py and run it with Python 3.12 or later:

python cancel_fence.py

It uses the standard library, a deterministic test clock and temporary SQLite files. No queue, cloud account or external API is required. The test that creates run-2 is setup for the old-request case; the earlier article covers acceptance of intentional reruns.

The write methods use short BEGIN IMMEDIATE transactions. SQLite allows one writer at a time, so cancellation and completion serialize before inspecting and changing the row. The transaction can still fail because another writer is busy or a database error occurs; those errors propagate instead of becoming a successful cancellation. SQLite documents these transaction rules.

"""A durable local cancellation boundary. Python 3.12+, standard library.
Run: python cancel_fence.py

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from contextlib import closing, contextmanager
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from threading import Barrier
import sqlite3
import tempfile
import unittest


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Claim:
    job_id: str
    run_id: str
    owner: str
    generation: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CancelResult:
    state: str
    changed: bool


class CompletionRefused(Exception):
    pass


class RunNotFound(Exception):
    pass


class Clock:
    def __init__(self, now=0):
        self.now = now

    def __call__(self):
        return self.now


def connect(path):
    db = sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=5, autocommit=True)
    db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return db


def one(db, sql, args=()):
    with closing(db.execute(sql, args)) as cursor:
        return cursor.fetchone()


@contextmanager
def transaction(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        try:
            db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE').close()
            yield db
            db.execute('COMMIT').close()
        except BaseException:
            if db.in_transaction:
                db.execute('ROLLBACK').close()
            raise


def initialize(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        db.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE runs (
            job_id TEXT NOT NULL, run_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            state TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued'
                CHECK (state IN ('queued', 'running', 'succeeded', 'cancelled')),
            generation INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
            owner TEXT, lease_until INTEGER, result TEXT,
            PRIMARY KEY (job_id, run_id)
        );
        INSERT INTO runs (job_id, run_id) VALUES ('report-1', 'run-1');
        """).close()


def claim_run(path, job_id, run_id, owner, clock, ttl=10):
    if type(ttl) is not int or ttl not in range(1, 3601):
        raise ValueError('TTL must be an integer in 1..3600')
    if not isinstance(owner, str) or not owner:
        raise ValueError('owner must be non-empty')
    with transaction(path) as db:
        now = clock()
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE runs
            SET state = 'running', owner = ?, lease_until = ?,
                generation = generation + 1
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?
              AND (state = 'queued' OR
                  (state = 'running' AND lease_until <= ?))""",
                (owner, now + ttl, job_id, run_id, now))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                return None
        generation = one(db, """SELECT generation FROM runs
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?""", (job_id, run_id))[0]
        return Claim(job_id, run_id, owner, generation)


def cancel_run(path, job_id, run_id):
    """Cancel this execution only. Does not kill a process or undo an effect."""
    with transaction(path) as db:
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE runs
            SET state = 'cancelled', owner = NULL, lease_until = NULL
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?
              AND state IN ('queued', 'running')""", (job_id, run_id))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount == 1:
                return CancelResult('cancelled', True)
        row = one(db, 'SELECT state FROM runs WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?',
                  (job_id, run_id))
        if row is None:
            raise RunNotFound((job_id, run_id))
        return CancelResult(row[0], False)


def complete_run(path, claim, result, clock):
    with transaction(path) as db:
        now = clock()
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE runs
            SET state = 'succeeded', result = ?, owner = NULL, lease_until = NULL
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ? AND state = 'running'
              AND owner = ? AND generation = ? AND lease_until > ?""",

                 claim.generation, now))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                raise CompletionRefused('claim expired, replaced or run terminal')
    return result

    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        with closing(db.execute('SELECT * FROM runs ORDER BY job_id, run_id')) as cur:
            return [dict(row) for row in cur.fetchall()]

    def setUp(self):
        base = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'test-db'
        base.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        self.temp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='cancel-', dir=base)
        assert Path(self.temp.name).resolve().is_relative_to(base.resolve())
        self.addCleanup(self.temp.cleanup)
        self.path = Path(self.temp.name) / 'runs.sqlite'
        self.clock = Clock()
        initialize(self.path)

    def claim(self, owner='worker-a', run='run-1'):
        return claim_run(self.path, 'report-1', run, owner, self.clock)

    def cancel(self, run='run-1'):
        return cancel_run(self.path, 'report-1', run)

        before = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertEqual(self.cancel(), CancelResult('succeeded', False))
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

        self.cancel()  # Pretend acknowledgement was lost.

        before = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertEqual(self.cancel(), CancelResult('cancelled', False))
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)
        complete_run(self.path, newer, 'new run result', self.clock)

        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(RunNotFound):
            cancel_run(self.path, 'other-job', 'run-1')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

        first = self.claim()
        self.clock.now = 10
        second = self.claim('worker-b')
        self.cancel()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        for token in (first, second):
            with self.assertRaises(CompletionRefused):
                complete_run(self.path, token, 'late', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_expiry_alone_is_not_cancelled_state(self):
        self.claim()
        self.clock.now = 10
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'running')
        second = self.claim('worker-b')
        complete_run(self.path, second, 'taken over', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'succeeded')

    def test_cancel_write_failure_is_not_reported_as_success(self):
        self.claim()
        with closing(connect(self.path)) as db:
            db.execute("""CREATE TRIGGER reject_cancel BEFORE UPDATE OF state ON runs
                WHEN NEW.state = 'cancelled'
                BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'injected failure'); END""").close()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(sqlite3.IntegrityError):
            self.cancel()
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def race(self, functions):
        barrier = Barrier(2)
        def run(fn):
            barrier.wait(timeout=5)
            return fn()
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
            return list(pool.map(run, functions))

    def test_concurrent_cancellers_have_one_transition(self):
        self.claim()
        outcomes = self.race([self.cancel, self.cancel])
        self.assertEqual(sum(r.changed for r in outcomes), 1)
        self.assertTrue(all(r.state == 'cancelled' for r in outcomes))

    def test_cancel_completion_race_agrees_with_committed_state(self):
        token = self.claim()
        def complete():
            try:
                complete_run(self.path, token, 'saved', self.clock)
                return 'accepted'
            except CompletionRefused:
                return 'refused'
        cancelled, completed = self.race([self.cancel, complete])
        row = snapshot(self.path)[0]
        if row['state'] == 'cancelled':
            self.assertTrue(cancelled.changed)
            self.assertEqual(completed, 'refused')
            self.assertIsNone(row['result'])
        else:
            self.assertEqual(cancelled, CancelResult('succeeded', False))
            self.assertEqual(completed, 'accepted')
            self.assertEqual(row['result'], 'saved')

    def test_negative_control_an_unguarded_writer_revives_cancelled_run(self):
        self.claim()
        self.cancel()
        # Deliberately unsafe control. Never expose this as a completion path.
        with transaction(self.path) as db:
            db.execute("""UPDATE runs SET state = 'succeeded', result = ?
                WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?""",
                ('late unsafe result', 'report-1', 'run-1')).close()
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'succeeded')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['result'], 'late unsafe result')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

Test the refusal and the unchanged row

The local run passed 12 tests. The deterministic cases force cancellation first and completion first separately. A barrier-based test then releases a canceller and a completer on separate connections and checks that their responses agree with the committed row, whichever wins.

Other tests cover a queued run, repeated cancellation after a lost response, an expired claim, takeover, a wrong job, a newer run, and a failure injected into the cancellation write.

The deliberately unsafe control is useful: an ID-only completion changes a cancelled row back to succeeded. That demonstrates why storing cancellation is insufficient when another write path ignores it. The guarded path refuses the late completion and leaves the cancelled row unchanged.

What an accepted cancel still cannot promise

There are three different observations an interface might show:

  1. Cancellation requested: the request has been sent, but no durable decision has been confirmed.
  2. Cancellation accepted: the run is terminal in the database, and its normal completion path is closed.
  3. Worker stopped: the worker has acknowledged shutdown or its process termination has been observed.

This fixture establishes the second observation. It does not implement the third. A separate cooperative signal can help the worker release resources earlier, but that signal should not be the only protection against a late write.

The guarantee is limited to the guarded database path. An email, webhook or file write performed beforehand is outside that transaction. A reversal or compensation is another operation with its own identity, authorization and outcome. Do not translate “local completion refused” into “nothing happened elsewhere.”

Production code also needs authenticated tenant/resource authorization, controlled database write permissions, a defined retention window, refusal auditing, and a trusted clock. The plain claim object assumes a trusted worker; it is not a signed capability. This example adds no shutdown handler, lease renewal or external-effect reconciler, and it makes no claim about SMTasker's internal implementation.

Which result does your Cancel button confirm: a request sent, a durable state change, or a worker that has actually stopped? Leave a race or retry case in the comments. The example is meant to make that promise testable.

            cancel_run(self.path, 'other-job', 'run-1')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_cancel_after_takeover_blocks_current_and_stale_workers(self):
        first = self.claim()
        self.clock.now = 10
        second = self.claim('worker-b')
        self.cancel()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        for token in (first, second):
            with self.assertRaises(CompletionRefused):
                complete_run(self.path, token, 'late', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_expiry_alone_is_not_cancelled_state(self):
        self.claim()
        self.clock.now = 10
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'running')
        second = self.claim('worker-b')
        complete_run(self.path, second, 'taken over', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'succeeded')

    def test_cancel_write_failure_is_not_reported_as_success(self):
        self.claim()
        with closing(connect(self.path)) as db:
            db.execute("""CREATE TRIGGER reject_cancel BEFORE UPDATE OF state ON runs
                WHEN NEW.state = 'cancelled'
                BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'injected failure'); END""").close()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(sqlite3.IntegrityError):
            self.cancel()
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def race(self, functions):
        barrier = Barrier(2)
        def run(fn):
            barrier.wait(timeout=5)
            return fn()
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
            return list(pool.map(run, functions))

    def test_concurrent_cancellers_have_one_transition(self):
        self.claim()
        outcomes = self.race([self.cancel, self.cancel])
        self.assertEqual(sum(r.changed for r in outcomes), 1)
        self.assertTrue(all(r.state == 'cancelled' for r in outcomes))

    def test_cancel_completion_race_agrees_with_committed_state(self):
        token = self.claim()
        def complete():
            try:
                complete_run(self.path, token, 'saved', self.clock)
                return 'accepted'
            except CompletionRefused:
                return 'refused'
        cancelled, completed = self.race([self.cancel, complete])
        row = snapshot(self.path)[0]
        if row['state'] == 'cancelled':
            self.assertTrue(cancelled.changed)
            self.assertEqual(completed, 'refused')
            self.assertIsNone(row['result'])
        else:
            self.assertEqual(cancelled, CancelResult('succeeded', False))
            self.assertEqual(completed, 'accepted')
            self.assertEqual(row['result'], 'saved')

    def test_negative_control_an_unguarded_writer_revives_cancelled_run(self):
        self.claim()
        self.cancel()
        # Deliberately unsafe control. Never expose this as a completion path.
        with transaction(self.path) as db:
            db.execute("""UPDATE runs SET state = 'succeeded', result = ?
                WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?""",
                ('late unsafe result', 'report-1', 'run-1')).close()
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'succeeded')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['result'], 'late unsafe result')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

Test the refusal and the unchanged row

The local run passed 12 tests. The deterministic cases force cancellation first and completion first separately. A barrier-based test then releases a canceller and a completer on separate connections and checks that their responses agree with the committed row, whichever wins.

Other tests cover a queued run, repeated cancellation after a lost response, an expired claim, takeover, a wrong job, a newer run, and a failure injected into the cancellation write.

The deliberately unsafe control is useful: an ID-only completion changes a cancelled row back to succeeded. That demonstrates why storing cancellation is insufficient when another write path ignores it. The guarded path refuses the late completion and leaves the cancelled row unchanged.

What an accepted cancel still cannot promise

There are three different observations an interface might show:

  1. Cancellation requested: the request has been sent, but no durable decision has been confirmed.
  2. Cancellation accepted: the run is terminal in the database, and its normal completion path is closed.
  3. Worker stopped: the worker has acknowledged shutdown or its process termination has been observed.

This fixture establishes the second observation. It does not implement the third. A separate cooperative signal can help the worker release resources earlier, but that signal should not be the only protection against a late write.

The guarantee is limited to the guarded database path. An email, webhook or file write performed beforehand is outside that transaction. A reversal or compensation is another operation with its own identity, authorization and outcome. Do not translate “local completion refused” into “nothing happened elsewhere.”

Production code also needs authenticated tenant/resource authorization, controlled database write permissions, a defined retention window, refusal auditing, and a trusted clock. The plain claim object assumes a trusted worker; it is not a signed capability. This example adds no shutdown handler, lease renewal or external-effect reconciler, and it makes no claim about SMTasker's internal implementation.

Which result does your Cancel button confirm: a request sent, a durable state change, or a worker that has actually stopped? Leave a race or retry case in the comments. The example is meant to make that promise testable.

title: How to Build a Voice AI Agent in 2026-2027: Pipecat vs LiveKit vs Vapi (Step-by-Step)
summary:
Your voice agent works in the demo. Then a real customer calls from an open-plan office.

The agent hears the caller. It also hears the colleague two desks away. It answers both, stops mid-sentence, and the call goes sideways.

If you're:

  • building your first voice agent and picking a framework,
  • moving a prototype from your laptop to real phone calls,
  • or choosing between Pipecat, LiveKit and Vapi,

this guide walks you through all three with the same agent, so you can compare them on code you can actually run.

Short answer: pick Pipecat if you want full control in open-source Python, LiveKit Agents if you want open-source code plus managed WebRTC and telephony, and Vapi if you want a hosted agent you configure instead of code. Whichever you pick, put Krisp voice isolation in front of the agent's ears. All three have a ready-made Krisp integration (on Pipecat, through Pipecat Cloud), and any other pipeline can call Krisp's standalone Voice Isolation API. In my LiveKit test recordings, it cut the words the agent picked up from a background voice from 224 to 35.

How a voice AI agent works

Every voice agent is the same pipeline, whatever framework you use:

  1. Transport brings the caller's audio in (WebRTC, a phone line, a browser).
  2. Voice isolation keeps the caller's voice and removes background voices and noise.
  3. VAD and turn detection decide when the caller is speaking and when they've finished.
  4. Speech-to-text (STT) turns the audio into words.
  5. The LLM decides what to say.
  6. Text-to-speech (TTS) speaks the answer back.

Some agents replace steps 4 to 6 with a single speech-to-speech model, which may also handle step 3. Others merge only part of the pipeline: Deepgram Flux, for example, builds turn detection into speech-to-text. Voice isolation can sit in front of either setup.

It's also the easiest step to leave out.

That's the step that decides whether the rest of the pipeline is working with the caller's words or with everyone in the room.

Speech-to-text handles noise well now. It still transcribes a second person talking near the mic, and the LLM answers it. In Krisp's test for its Voice Isolation 2.5 release, 10 speech-to-text systems averaged 2.10% word error rate on clean single-speaker audio and 35.92% with a second person talking. With Voice Isolation 2.5 in front, that 35.92% fell to 10.90% (release post).

Pipecat vs LiveKit vs Vapi: which one to pick

The three tools sit at different levels of control:

Pipecat LiveKit Agents Vapi

You write The whole pipeline, frame by frame An agent class and a session config A JSON assistant config
Hosting Anywhere, or Pipecat Cloud LiveKit Cloud or self-hosted Vapi
STT / LLM / TTS Bring your own providers Your own keys, or LiveKit Inference (no provider keys) Picked in the config, billed through Vapi
Krisp voice isolation KrispVivaFilter on Pipecat Cloud; Krisp's Voice Isolation API (or a licensed SDK) for local pipelines krisp.voice_isolation() plugin Smart Denoising, one config field
Best for Teams that want full control over every frame Teams that want code plus managed real-time infrastructure Teams that want an agent live without running servers

I built the same agent on each one: Ava, a support agent for an online store that answers order-status questions in one or two sentences.

1. Build a voice agent with Pipecat

Pipecat is the most hands-on option. You assemble a pipeline of processors and Pipecat moves audio and text frames through it.

I used pipecat-ai 1.16.0 and OpenAI for all three AI services, so the only key needed is OPENAI_API_KEY.

pip install "pipecat-ai[openai,silero,webrtc,runner]" python-dotenv

import os
from pipecat.audio.vad.silero import SileroVADAnalyzer
from pipecat.frames.frames import LLMRunFrame
from pipecat.pipeline.pipeline import Pipeline
from pipecat.pipeline.runner import PipelineRunner
from pipecat.pipeline.task import PipelineParams, PipelineTask
from pipecat.processors.aggregators.llm_context import LLMContext
from pipecat.processors.aggregators.llm_response_universal import LLMContextAggregatorPair, LLMUserAggregatorParams
from pipecat.runner.types import RunnerArguments
from pipecat.runner.utils import create_transport
from pipecat.services.openai.llm import OpenAILLMService
from pipecat.services.openai.stt import OpenAISTTService
from pipecat.services.openai.tts import OpenAITTSService
from pipecat.transports.base_transport import TransportParams

# Krisp VIVA ships preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud; locally the import fails and the bot runs without it
try:
    from pipecat.audio.filters.krisp_viva_filter import KrispVivaFilter
    krisp_filter = KrispVivaFilter()
except Exception:
    krisp_filter = None

INSTRUCTIONS = ("You are Ava, a support agent for an online store. Keep answers short: one or two sentences, "
                "spoken style. If the caller gives an order number, say it is out for delivery today.")
